questions.stem: Relative isotopic masses are measured on a scale based on which standard?
options: The hydrogen-1 isotope, assigned a mass of exactly 1
The oxygen-16 isotope, assigned a mass of exactly 16
The average mass of a carbon atom, assigned exactly 12
The carbon-12 isotope, assigned a mass of exactly 12
questions.explanation: The mass of a carbon-12 atom is defined as exactly 12, and every other isotope's mass is measured relative to it. The average mass of natural carbon atoms is slightly more than 12, because natural carbon also contains carbon-13.

questions.stem: Why is the relative atomic mass of carbon slightly more than 12 rather than exactly 12?
options: Carbon's mass is measured relative to hydrogen-1, which is not an exact standard
Natural carbon is a mixture of isotopes, mostly carbon-12 with some carbon-13
Carbon-12 atoms have slightly more mass than the standard they are compared with
Carbon atoms gain electrons during measurement, which adds a little mass
questions.explanation: Relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the relative isotopic masses of an element's naturally occurring isotopes. Carbon-12 is exactly 12 by definition, so the small amount of heavier carbon-13 lifts the average a little above 12. The scale is based on carbon-12, not hydrogen-1.

questions.stem: In the mass spectrum of an element, what does the relative height of each peak show?
options: The relative isotopic mass of each isotope
The number of protons in each isotope
The number of electrons lost by each isotope
The relative abundance of each isotope
questions.explanation: Each peak sits at the relative isotopic mass of one isotope, read from the horizontal axis. Its height shows how common that isotope is. The relative atomic mass is then the average of the isotopic masses weighted by these abundances.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of boron shows boron-10 (relative isotopic mass 10.0, abundance 20.0%) and boron-11 (11.0, abundance 80.0%). What is the relative atomic mass of boron?
questions.explanation: Ar = (10.0 × 20.0 + 11.0 × 80.0) ÷ 100 = (200 + 880) ÷ 100 = 10.8. 10.5 is a plain average that ignores the abundances, and 10.2 swaps the abundances of the two isotopes.

questions.stem: Chlorine has two isotopes, with relative isotopic masses of 35.0 and 37.0. Its relative atomic mass is 35.5. What is the percentage abundance of chlorine-35?
questions.explanation: Let x be the fraction of chlorine-35: 35.0x + 37.0(1 − x) = 35.5, so 37.0 − 2.0x = 35.5 and x = 0.75. The average is much closer to 35 than to 37, so chlorine-35 must be the more abundant isotope; 25% is the abundance of chlorine-37.

questions.stem: How many molecules are in 2.00 mol of carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: N = n × NA = 2.00 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.20 × 10²⁴ molecules. 3.61 × 10²⁴ is the number of atoms, since each CO₂ molecule contains three atoms.

questions.stem: What amount of carbon dioxide, in mol, is in 11.0 g of the gas?
questions.explanation: M(CO₂) = 12.0 + 2 × 16.0 = 44.0 g mol⁻¹, so n = m ÷ M = 11.0 ÷ 44.0 = 0.250 mol. 4.00 mol comes from dividing the molar mass by the mass, and 484 from multiplying them.

questions.stem: How many hydrogen atoms are in 9.0 g of water?
questions.explanation: n(H₂O) = 9.0 ÷ 18.0 = 0.50 mol, so there are 0.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules. Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms, giving 6.02 × 10²³ hydrogen atoms. 3.01 × 10²³ counts molecules, and 9.03 × 10²³ counts all atoms, including oxygen.

questions.stem: What is the molar mass of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂?
questions.explanation: M = 40.1 + 2 × (14.0 + 3 × 16.0) = 40.1 + 2 × 62.0 = 164.1 g mol⁻¹. 102.1 counts only one nitrate ion, and 116.1 applies the 2 to nitrogen but not to the oxygen atoms inside the bracket.

questions.stem: What is the percentage by mass of carbon in ethanol, C₂H₆O?
questions.explanation: M(C₂H₆O) = 2 × 12.0 + 6 × 1.0 + 16.0 = 46.0 g mol⁻¹, and carbon contributes 24.0 g mol⁻¹, so %C = 24.0 ÷ 46.0 × 100 = 52.2%. 22.2% is the fraction of atoms that are carbon (2 of 9), not the fraction of mass, and 26.1% counts only one carbon atom.

questions.stem: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. What is its empirical formula?
questions.explanation: In 100 g there are 40.0 ÷ 12.0 = 3.33 mol C, 6.7 ÷ 1.0 = 6.7 mol H and 53.3 ÷ 16.0 = 3.33 mol O. Dividing by the smallest, 3.33, gives a ratio of 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O. Using the percentages directly as a ratio, without dividing by the molar masses, gives a wrong answer.

questions.stem: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon by mass and has a molar mass of 56.0 g mol⁻¹. What is its molecular formula?
questions.explanation: Moles in 100 g: C = 85.7 ÷ 12.0 = 7.14 and H = 14.3 ÷ 1.0 = 14.3, a 1 : 2 ratio, so the empirical formula is CH₂ (14.0 g mol⁻¹). 56.0 ÷ 14.0 = 4, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈. CH₂ is only the empirical formula, and C₄H₁₀ has a molar mass of 58.0 g mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Which general formula represents the alkenes with one carbon–carbon double bond?
questions.explanation: An alkene has two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbons, so its formula is CnH2n, as in ethene, C₂H₄. CnH2n+2 is the alkanes, and the other two are the alcohols and carboxylic acids.

questions.stem: Butane (58 g mol⁻¹) boils at about 0 °C, while propan-1-ol (60 g mol⁻¹) boils at 97 °C. What best explains the difference?
options: Butane molecules are polar, so they repel each other and separate easily
Propan-1-ol contains ions that attract one another strongly in the liquid
Propan-1-ol molecules form hydrogen bonds through their hydroxyl groups
Propan-1-ol has a larger molar mass, so its dispersion forces are much stronger
questions.explanation: The molecules have almost the same molar mass, so their dispersion forces are similar. The O–H group of the alcohol forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, which need much more energy to overcome. Butane is non-polar, and alcohols are molecular, not ionic.

questions.stem: Which family of organic compounds gives vinegar its sour taste and forms acidic solutions in water?
questions.explanation: Vinegar is a dilute solution of ethanoic acid, a carboxylic acid. The –COOH group can donate a hydrogen ion to water, so the solutions are acidic. Alcohols contain an O–H group but are not acidic in water.

questions.stem: Why are alkenes more reactive than alkanes?
options: Their molecules are polar, so they attract other reactants more strongly
Their molecules are larger, so dispersion forces pull reactants closer
Their C=C double bond lets other atoms add across it in addition reactions
Their C–H bonds are weaker, so their hydrogen atoms are lost more easily
questions.explanation: The double bond in an alkene is a site where one of the bonds can open and new atoms, such as hydrogen or bromine, can join the carbons. Alkanes have only single bonds and react mainly by combustion. Simple alkenes are non-polar, like alkanes.

questions.stem: Chlorofluorocarbons, a group of haloalkanes, were once widely used as refrigerants. Which properties made them suitable?
options: They are unreactive, non-flammable and boil at low temperatures
They react readily with water, absorbing heat as they do so
They are ionic, so they conduct heat well through the pipes
They have very high boiling points, so they rarely evaporate
questions.explanation: A refrigerant must evaporate and condense easily, so a low boiling point is needed, and being unreactive and non-flammable made CFCs safe to use. Their stability later proved a problem, because it let them reach the upper atmosphere. Haloalkanes are molecular, not ionic.

questions.stem: Ethanol is used as a solvent in perfumes and hand sanitisers. Which feature of its structure lets it dissolve both polar and some non-polar substances?
options: A carboxyl group that ionises completely when it is in water
A fully non-polar molecule that is too small to form any dipoles
A polar hydroxyl group attached to a non-polar hydrocarbon chain
An ionic O–H bond attached to a polar carbon–carbon double bond
questions.explanation: The –OH end of ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water and other polar molecules, while the CH₃CH₂– part attracts non-polar molecules through dispersion forces. Ethanol has no double bond and no carboxyl group, and its O–H bond is polar covalent, not ionic.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: There are five carbon atoms in a chain, all joined by single bonds, so the stem is pent- and the ending is -ane. Butane has four carbons, and pent-1-ene would need a C=C double bond.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain has four carbons, so the parent is butane, with a methyl branch. Numbering from the end nearer the branch puts it on carbon 2. 3-methylbutane numbers from the wrong end, and 2-ethylpropane misses that the longest chain runs through the ethyl group.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂OH?
questions.explanation: Three carbons give the stem propan-, and the hydroxyl group on the end carbon is numbered 1, giving propan-1-ol. Numbering should give the functional group the lowest number, so propan-3-ol is wrong. Propan-2-ol has the OH group on the middle carbon.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: Four carbons with a C=C double bond make a butene. The double bond starts at carbon 1 when the chain is numbered from the end nearer to it, so the name is but-1-ene. But-3-ene numbers from the wrong end, and but-2-ene has the double bond between the middle carbons.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The chain has four carbons and the chlorine atom is on the second carbon from the nearer end, so the name is 2-chlorobutane. 3-chlorobutane numbers from the far end. 2-chloropropane would have only three carbons.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂COOH?
questions.explanation: The carbon of the –COOH group is counted in the chain, so there are three carbons and the acid is propanoic acid. Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, comes from forgetting to count the carboxyl carbon.

questions.stem: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₅H₁₂?
questions.explanation: The isomers are pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane. Drawings such as 3-methylbutane or a bent chain of five carbons are the same molecules drawn differently, which is why students often count too many.

questions.stem: A student named a compound 2-ethylbutane. What is its correct IUPAC name?
questions.explanation: Drawing 2-ethylbutane shows that the longest chain runs from the end of the ethyl group through carbon 2 to carbon 4, which is five carbons. A methyl branch sits on the third carbon of that chain, so the name is 3-methylpentane. 2-methylpentane is a different isomer with the branch one carbon nearer the end.

questions.stem: Which semi-structural formula represents butan-2-ol?
questions.explanation: Butan-2-ol has four carbons with the OH group on carbon 2. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH is butan-1-ol, and CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ has five carbons, so it is pentan-3-ol.

questions.stem: Which pair of compounds are structural isomers?
questions.explanation: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but a different arrangement of atoms. Butane and 2-methylpropane are both C₄H₁₀. Pentane is C₅H₁₂ while 2-methylpentane is C₆H₁₄, so despite their similar names they are not isomers.

questions.stem: Why is plant-based biomass described as a renewable source of organic chemicals?
options: It can be regrown within a human lifetime, unlike crude oil
It contains no carbon, so it releases no CO₂ when it is used
It forms from fossil fuels over millions of years underground
Its chemicals are always less toxic than those from crude oil
questions.explanation: Crops and plant waste can be grown again season after season, whereas crude oil took millions of years to form and is being used far faster than it forms. Biomass is made of carbon compounds, and a chemical's toxicity depends on its structure, not on whether it came from plants or oil.

questions.stem: Many organic solvents in paints and adhesives are volatile. Which hazard does this create?
options: They react with water in the air to form strong acids
They form solid precipitates on contact with the skin
Their vapours can be breathed in and may catch fire
They conduct electricity and can give electric shocks
questions.explanation: A volatile liquid evaporates easily, so its vapour reaches the air people breathe, and many organic solvent vapours are flammable. This is why these products are used in well-ventilated areas away from flames. Organic solvents are molecular and do not conduct electricity.

questions.stem: Some pesticides are non-polar organic compounds that break down slowly. Why can they build up in the fatty tissue of animals?
options: Fat cells convert the pesticides into charged ions that cannot leave the body
Non-polar molecules dissolve in fats rather than water, so they are not easily excreted
Polar molecules dissolve in water, so they are carried into the fat cells and stored
Non-polar molecules form ionic bonds with the proteins found inside fat cells
questions.explanation: Like dissolves like: non-polar pesticides dissolve in non-polar fats but not in the water of blood and urine, so they are stored rather than excreted. Each animal that eats contaminated food takes in more, so concentrations can rise up a food chain. Non-polar molecules do not form ionic bonds.

questions.stem: What distinguishes condensation polymerisation from addition polymerisation?
options: The monomers must each contain a carbon–carbon double bond
The polymer it forms is always a thermosetting plastic
The monomers join without forming any new covalent bonds
A small molecule such as water is released as each link forms
questions.explanation: In condensation polymerisation two functional groups react to join the monomers, releasing a small molecule such as water each time. Addition polymerisation needs C=C double bonds and gives the polymer as the only product. Both processes join monomers by covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Which monomer is used to make poly(vinyl chloride), PVC?
questions.explanation: Addition polymers form from monomers with a C=C double bond, and PVC's repeating unit, –CH₂–CHCl–, comes from chloroethene. Chloroethane has only single bonds, so it cannot undergo addition polymerisation. Ethene and propene make polyethene and polypropene.

questions.stem: Which is the repeating unit of polypropene, made from propene, CH₂=CHCH₃?
questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation the C=C double bond opens and the two carbons of the double bond join the chain, so the CH₃ group becomes a branch. Writing all three carbons in the chain ignores where the double bond was. No double bond remains in the polymer.

questions.stem: A plastic softens when heated and can be remoulded into a new shape. Which best describes its structure?
options: A lattice of positive and negative ions in fixed positions
Chains of carbon atoms held together by metallic bonding
Linear chains held to each other only by intermolecular forces
Chains joined to each other by covalent cross-links throughout
questions.explanation: A thermoplastic is made of linear chains attracted by intermolecular forces. Heating overcomes these forces, so the chains can slide past each other and set in a new shape on cooling. Covalent cross-links describe a thermosetting polymer, which does not soften.

questions.stem: Why can thermosetting polymers not be recycled by melting and remoulding?
options: Their linear chains slide apart too easily when heated to hold any new shape
Their chains are joined by covalent cross-links, which break only when the polymer decomposes
Their chains are held only by weak dispersion forces, which break at a low temperature
Their monomers are released as gases as soon as the plastic starts to be heated
questions.explanation: Cross-links are strong covalent bonds that hold the chains in a rigid network. Heating does not let the chains move apart; at high temperatures the polymer chars and decomposes instead of melting. Chains held only by intermolecular forces describe a thermoplastic, which can be remelted.

questions.stem: HDPE has fewer branches on its chains than LDPE. Why is HDPE denser and more rigid?
options: Its chains are cross-linked by covalent bonds that the chains of LDPE do not have
Its branches form hydrogen bonds that hold neighbouring chains further apart
Its chains contain more C=C double bonds, which are stronger than single bonds
Its chains pack more closely, so the dispersion forces between them are stronger
questions.explanation: Unbranched chains can line up and pack tightly, so more mass fits in each volume and the dispersion forces between chains are stronger, making the plastic rigid. Branches in LDPE keep chains apart. Both are linear polyethene, with no cross-links and no remaining double bonds.

questions.stem: How does increasing the average chain length of a linear addition polymer affect its properties?
options: It becomes more polar, because each extra carbon atom adds a permanent dipole
Its melting point and strength increase, because dispersion forces between chains are stronger
Its melting point decreases, because longer chains are more tangled and pack less well
It becomes thermosetting, because the longer chains form covalent cross-links
questions.explanation: Longer chains have more electrons and more contact with neighbouring chains, so the total dispersion forces are greater and more energy is needed to separate them. Chain length alone does not create cross-links. Adding CH₂ units to a hydrocarbon chain does not make it polar.

questions.stem: A designer wants a linear addition polymer with stronger forces between its chains than polyethene. Which monomer is the best choice?
options: But-1-ene, as its ethyl branches let the chains pack together more tightly
Ethanol, as its O–H groups form hydrogen bonds between neighbouring chains
Chloroethene, as polar C–Cl bonds add dipole-dipole attraction between chains
Ethane, as its single bonds can link the chains together more strongly
questions.explanation: Chloroethene has a C=C double bond, so it forms an addition polymer, and its polar C–Cl bonds give dipole-dipole attractions as well as dispersion forces. Ethane and ethanol have no C=C bond, so they cannot form addition polymers. Branches push chains apart rather than letting them pack tightly.

questions.stem: Which of these plastics is a bioplastic?
questions.explanation: PLA is made from lactic acid produced by fermenting plant sugars or starch, so its raw material is renewable. PVC, HDPE and PS are made from monomers obtained from fossil fuels.

questions.stem: Bio-PE is made from ethene produced from sugarcane ethanol. Compared with polyethene made from crude oil, Bio-PE is:
options: a condensation polymer, because water is formed as it is made
a thermosetting polymer, because its plant chains are cross-linked
chemically identical, but made from a renewable raw material
biodegradable, because it is made from a plant-based material
questions.explanation: Once the ethene has been made, it polymerises in exactly the same way whatever its source, so Bio-PE has the same structure and properties as fossil-based polyethene. That means it is not biodegradable just because it came from plants. Addition polymerisation of ethene releases no water.

questions.stem: Which process is mechanical recycling of a plastic?
options: Breaking the polymer down into its monomers using chemical reactions
Composting a biodegradable plastic so microbes can break it down
Burning the plastic to recover its energy for making electricity
Sorting, shredding and remelting a thermoplastic to make new products
questions.explanation: Mechanical recycling keeps the polymer chains intact: the plastic is cleaned, shredded and melted into new items, which only works for thermoplastics. Breaking chains into monomers is chemical recycling, and composting is organic recycling.

questions.stem: PLA is described as compostable, yet it often does not break down in a home compost bin. Why?
options: It is made from crude oil, so the microbes in compost cannot digest its chains
It is a thermosetting polymer, so its cross-links protect it from the microbes
It is an addition polymer, so it has no links in its chains that can be hydrolysed
It breaks down at a useful rate only at the high temperatures of industrial composting
questions.explanation: PLA's ester links are hydrolysed and then digested by microbes, but this is very slow at the temperatures of a home compost heap. Industrial composting facilities run much hotter, which speeds the breakdown greatly. PLA is a plant-based condensation polymer, not an oil-based addition polymer.

questions.stem: PLA can be made by condensation polymerisation of lactic acid. Which small molecule is released as each link forms?
questions.explanation: Lactic acid has both a hydroxyl group and a carboxyl group. The –OH of one molecule reacts with the –COOH of the next, forming an ester link and releasing a water molecule each time.

questions.stem: How does the hydrolysis of condensation polymers such as PLA support a transition towards a circular economy?
options: Adding water breaks the links between monomers, which can then be recovered and repolymerised
Removing water joins the monomers again, so the polymer gets stronger each time it is reused
Adding water dissolves the polymer, so it can be poured straight into new moulds
Heating with water breaks the C=C double bonds, so the chains become shorter and reusable
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation: water reacts at each link, splitting the polymer back into its monomers. Recovered monomers can be made into new polymer, keeping the material in use instead of sending it to landfill. Condensation polymers have no C=C double bonds in their chains.
